final.memo:
Sony is a storied company and a global leader in entertainment and technology, yet it remains a classic example of a bloated conglomerate where the crown jewels—its high-margin entertainment and music businesses—are obscured by the underperforming electronics division [D01, D03, D05]. The market currently fails to recognize the inherent value of these assets, leaving the company trading at a 0.85x price-to-book ratio, which we believe fundamentally misprices the sum of its parts [D01, D04].

Our sum-of-the-parts analysis confirms the significant valuation gap. We value the entertainment and music units at approximately ¥1.5 trillion, while the electronics and other assets are valued at ¥1.3 trillion [D01, D03]. After accounting for ¥356.2 billion in net debt, we arrive at a per-share valuation of ¥2,750, a meaningful premium to the current price of ¥1,855 [D04].

The market’s pessimism is rooted in the lackluster 3.4% operating margin of the consolidated entity, which compares poorly against peers like Canon at 9.3% [D03, D06]. We believe this margin drag is a result of the conglomerate structure rather than the quality of the individual assets [D03, D05]. A structural separation will clarify value, improve capital discipline, and allow the content assets to be valued more in line with their Western peers [D01, D03].

We are calling for a spin-off or a minority IPO of up to 20% of the entertainment business [D03]. This is a targeted, executable plan that allows CEO Kazuo Hirai and the board to surface value without surrendering control [D03]. Our role will be to apply constructive, public pressure through a clear, evidence-based campaign to ensure the board prioritizes this initiative over the next three quarters [D03, D05].

The primary risks involve management entrenchment and the potential for a drawn-out governance battle [D05]. We acknowledge that electronics competition is fierce and the hit-driven nature of content earnings presents volatility [D05]. However, the 0.85x price-to-book floor provides us with a margin of safety, and we believe the upside skew of 48% versus 15% downside justifies our conviction [D03, D04].

We are initiating a position in Sony common shares, with an initial target of 5% of NAV. We will size the position to reflect our high conviction in the catalyst, while utilizing index puts on the Nikkei 225 to hedge against systemic Japanese market volatility [D05, D07]. We exit if management explicitly rejects the proposal or if the thesis breaks [D03, D05].
